theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: On a three-day rewiring job in an occupied office, what housekeeping should be planned for the end of each day?
options: Leave it safe: ends made safe, covers on, area tidy
Leave tools on the desks so work starts faster
Leave the waste in a corner to clear on day three
Leave the boards open so the staff can see progress

questions.stem: At the end of the day a new circuit is not finished. How should its loose cable ends be left?
options: Connected to the board so they can be tested
Isolated, with ends insulated and coiled safely
Pushed up into the ceiling out of sight
Taped to the wall with a bit of copper still showing

questions.stem: A breaker has been taken out of a board, leaving a gap in the cover. Why must the gap be closed with a blank?
options: So the board looks complete to the client
So dust cannot settle on the cover's paint
So no one can touch live parts through it
So the other breakers do not move about

questions.stem: Metal filings fall into a distribution board while a hole is drilled in it. Why must they be removed before switch-on?
options: They make the board heavier to fix
They change the colour of the busbars
They stop the cover from closing properly on the board
They can cause short circuits or tracking

questions.stem: Which is the better way to clean dust out of an isolated control panel, and why?
options: A vacuum, so dust is removed, not blown into parts
Compressed air, so dust is blown into the corners
A wet cloth, so that the dust turns into a paste and sticks
A wire brush, so the dust is pushed down

questions.stem: A store is short of space. Which place must NOT be used to store cable drums?
options: On a rack beside the back wall
In front of the main switchboard
On chocks in the drum bay
On a pallet in the yard store

questions.stem: Why should copper scrap be kept in a secure, marked container at the Centre?
options: Copper scrap goes bad if it is left in the air
So the copper can be reused as new cable later
It has resale value and is a target for theft
So the copper can be burned off safely later

questions.stem: Why must fluorescent tubes be kept whole when they are taken out?
options: So they can be put back in again later
So they fit better in the general waste skip at the back
So the glass can be sold as new tubes
Broken tubes release harmful vapour and sharp glass

questions.stem: Which waste from an electrical job should go for e-waste or special collection?
options: Old LED drivers, meters and circuit boards
Cardboard boxes from the new fittings
Short offcuts of PVC conduit
Bags of plaster dust from chasing

questions.stem: A job leaves a lot of cardboard and plastic packaging from light fittings. What is best?
options: Leave it in the room for the client's cleaner
Flatten and bag it as the work goes, for recycling
Push it up into the ceiling space out of sight
Burn it all at the back of the building after work is done

questions.stem: Apart from tripping, why are trailing extension leads a hazard?
options: They make the lights in the room flicker
They use more electricity when they lie on the floor
They get crushed or cut, exposing live parts
They change the voltage of the outlets

questions.stem: Why must a cable-reel extension lead be fully unwound before a heavy load is run from it?
options: So it reaches the farthest corner
So its colour can be seen easily
So no one trips over the reel left on the floor
A wound reel can overheat and melt

questions.stem: Why must water never be used on a fire in a live distribution board?
options: Water conducts and can give a fatal shock
Water makes the fire smell worse
Water will rust the board's cover
Water is far too slow to put out any kind of fire

questions.stem: Why should dust, paper and cardboard not be left against light fittings and boards?
options: They will block the light from the room
Heat from the equipment can set them alight
They make the equipment harder to label
The client will think the job is unfinished

questions.stem: Chasing a block wall makes heavy dust. Which step best protects other people in the building?
options: Sweep it up with a dry broom at the end
Open the doors so the dust spreads out
Use dust extraction and clean up with a vacuum
Wet the dust down with a hose so that it settles on the floor

questions.stem: Why should a wet mop not be used around open boards and floor outlets?
options: The mop head will wear out more quickly near the boards
The floor will take too long to dry
The cleaner will damage the paint
Water near live parts can give a shock

questions.stem: How should contact cleaner and isopropyl alcohol be stored in the workshop?
options: Closed, labelled, away from heat, well ventilated
In open trays on the bench, ready to use
Poured into drink bottles to save space
On the top of the distribution board

questions.stem: Why should cleaning sprays not be used on equipment that is still live?
options: They work better on warm equipment
Many are flammable, and can cause tracking or shock
They will remove all the printed labels from the equipment
Live equipment does not need any cleaning

questions.stem: A little battery acid spills on the battery room floor. What should be done?
options: Wash it into the drain with plenty of water
Wipe it up with a bare hand and a rag
Use the spill kit and neutraliser, as the SDS says
Leave it to dry out by itself overnight

questions.stem: How should part-used coils of cable be stored?
options: Loose on the floor, ready for the next job
Stuffed into a drum with other cables
Hung from the ceiling on a hook
Coiled, tied, labelled and kept on a rack

questions.stem: How should 3 m lengths of conduit be stored in the store room?
options: Flat on a rack, not leaning against a wall
Upright in a corner, leaning on each other
Across two chairs in the workshop
On the floor along the main walkway

questions.stem: How should ladders be stored at the Centre?
options: Standing open in the workshop corner
Flat on wall brackets, out of sun and rain
Leaning on the outside wall of the building
Laid on the ground behind the store

questions.stem: Why should the bins of fittings in the electrical store be labelled with size and type?
options: So the store looks colourful and bright
So the bins can be stacked higher up
So the right part is found quickly, not mixed
So the fittings cannot be used by other trainees or staff

questions.stem: Why should tools not be left on top of ladders or in ceiling spaces?
options: They will get too hot up there
They make the ladder unsteady to climb
Someone may borrow them without asking
They can fall on someone or be left behind

questions.stem: During a housekeeping check you find a cracked outlet cover in the workshop. What should you do?
options: Tag it out of use and report it for repair
Tape over the crack and carry on working
Leave it, as it still works when used
Push furniture in front of the outlet

questions.stem: A housekeeping check finds the same untidy bench three weeks in a row. What should the team leader do?
options: Tidy the bench again and say nothing
Find out why and agree a fix with its users
Remove the bench from the workshop
Stop doing checks on that bench

questions.stem: Out of 55 items on the electrical workshop checklist, 44 are marked OK. What percentage are OK?
You are working in a classroom while lessons go on next door. Which housekeeping step matters most?
options: Leave the doors open so that the students can watch
Put the waste in the students' bins
Clean up only at the end of the week
Keep everything inside a barriered work area

questions.stem: Before leaving a client's home for the day, what must you tell them?
options: Which circuits are off and what is safe to use
How much the job will cost per hour
Which tools you will bring the next day
How long the cable runs were in metres

questions.stem: A hole is left in a ceiling for work the next day. What housekeeping step is needed?
options: Nothing, as the work starts again tomorrow
Cover or barrier it, with a warning sign
Fill it with the cable offcuts
Put the ladder under it for tomorrow

questions.stem: A fluorescent tube breaks on the floor. Which clean-up method is right?
options: Vacuum it up straight away with the shop vacuum cleaner
Sweep it into the general bin with a broom
Air the room; lift it with card and tape into a bag
Leave it until the end of the day

questions.stem: In 5S, which step means putting each size of crimp terminal in its own labelled drawer?
options: Sort
Shine
Sustain
Set in order

questions.stem: Who is responsible for keeping an electrician's own work area tidy during a job?
options: Each worker, all the time
The client's cleaner, once a day
The supervisor, at the end of the job
The security guard, after hours

questions.stem: A light over a workshop bench has failed. Why is reporting it part of housekeeping?
options: So the electricity bill comes down
Poor light leads to mistakes and accidents
So the bench can be moved somewhere else in the room
So the room is darker for the projector

questions.stem: Cable drums have been left in the workshop walkway. What is the problem?
options: They make the cable cold
They hide the floor markings
They block escape routes and can roll
They make the workshop look busy

questions.stem: Why must the isolator for the workshop's machines be easy to reach and never blocked?
options: So visitors can see it on a tour
So it can be painted each year
So it is easy to label correctly
So power can be cut fast in an emergency

questions.stem: Old lead-acid batteries from a standby system must be disposed of. Which is right?
options: Return them to a licensed recycler or supplier
Put them in the general skip with the rubbish
Bury them behind the workshop
Empty the acid down a drain first

questions.stem: A trainee leaves stripped insulation and offcuts on the floor round the training bay. What should you do as team leader?
options: Clean it up for him at the end of the day
Explain the slip risk and have him clear as he goes
Tell the cleaner to sweep the bay more often
Move his training bay to the back corner

questions.stem: Why are test instruments put back in their cases with their leads checked at the end of each day?
options: So they look neat on the shelf
So their batteries can charge up overnight in the case
So they stay accurate and safe for the next user
So the leads can be used for other jobs

questions.stem: On a building site, why should cable and tools be locked away each night?
options: So the site looks empty and tidy to the client
So the tools are cool in the morning
So the cable does not get dusty
To stop theft and unsafe use by others

questions.stem: Which is the right way to deal with leftover PVC conduit when a wiring job is finished?
options: Keep useful lengths; put the rest in the right bin
Leave them in the ceiling for the next electrician
Burn them in an old drum at the back of the site
Throw them over the fence into the gully

questions.stem: Why must cable sheath and PVC offcuts never be burned on site?
options: The smoke attracts too much attention
Burning PVC gives off toxic, corrosive fumes
The copper inside will melt and be lost
Burning it makes the fire too small

questions.stem: A roof leak is dripping near the workshop's distribution board. What should you do first?
options: Wipe the board dry with a cloth
Put a bucket on top of the board
Keep people away, isolate if safe, and report it
Carry on working, as the board has a metal cover on it

questions.stem: Why should an isolated light fitting be cleaned when its lamps are changed?
options: So the new lamps fit properly into the lamp holders
So the fitting's guarantee is kept
So the lamp's colour changes to white
Dust cuts the light output and traps heat

questions.stem: What is the last check before the electrical workshop is locked at the end of the day?
options: Equipment off, isolators set, area safe and tidy
The bins are full so they can be emptied tomorrow
All the lights are left on for the guard
The doors are open to let air through

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the plate fitted in a board cover where a breaker has been removed?
Name the extinguisher, by the gas inside it, that is commonly used on fires in electrical equipment.
Which toxic metal inside fluorescent tubes makes them hazardous waste?
Which white household powder is often used to neutralise small battery acid spills, where the SDS allows it?
A housekeeping checklist has 50 items and 43 of them pass. What percentage pass?
What short name is given to waste such as old circuit boards, electronic drivers and meters?
What name is given to the clear space that must be kept in front of a switchboard so people can work on it and get away safely?
What is the name of the insulated cap or connector put on a bare conductor end to cover it until the work is finished?
What word describes waste that can harm people or the environment, such as tubes, batteries and solvents, and so needs special disposal?
A skip holds 6 m³. A job makes 0.75 m³ of waste a day. After how many days will the skip be full?
What do we call the area marked off with barriers or tape round the work, to keep other people out?
Should the vacuum nozzle used inside an isolated board be metal or non-metallic?
Which flammable gas can build up near charging lead-acid batteries, so the area must be ventilated?
38 kg of copper scrap is sold at J$900 per kg (a made-up price). How much is that in J$?
What short phrase describes clearing waste and tools as the work goes on, rather than leaving it to the end?

essays.stem: Describe how you would leave an unfinished electrical installation safe and tidy at the end of each day on a job in an occupied building.
essays.modelAnswer: I plan to stop about half an hour early to make the work safe. Any circuit that is being worked on stays isolated, locked off and tagged, or new cables are left disconnected with their ends insulated and coiled safely, never with bare copper showing. Covers and lids go back on boxes and boards, and blanking plates fill any gaps where breakers are missing. Holes in ceilings or floors are covered or barriered with a warning. Tools, ladders and materials are removed or locked away, and leads are unplugged and coiled. Waste is bagged and taken to the right bins, and dust is vacuumed. Finally I check that the circuits the client needs are working, tell the person in charge what is off and what is safe to use, and note it in the job diary.
markingPoints: Circuits isolated, locked and tagged, or ends insulated
Covers on, blanks fitted, holes covered
Tools, ladders and materials removed or locked away
Waste removed and area cleaned
Checks supplies and tells the person in charge what is off

essays.stem: Explain how to clean the inside of a distribution board or control panel safely, before it is energised or during maintenance.
essays.modelAnswer: First the board is isolated at its supply, locked off and tagged, and proved dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. I remember that some parts, such as incoming terminals, may still be live if the board is fed from elsewhere, so I keep clear of them. I remove the covers and look for filings, offcuts, dust, insects and nests. I use a vacuum cleaner with a non-metallic nozzle and a soft brush to lift dirt, rather than compressed air, which blows dust into the parts. Any cleaning spray is used only as the maker and the SDS allow, with good ventilation. I check that no tools or offcuts are left inside, count my tools, refit all covers and blanks, and record the work before the board is re-energised by the authorised person.
markingPoints: Safe isolation with tester checked before and after
Awareness of parts that may still be live
Vacuum with non-metallic nozzle and brush; not compressed air
Cleaning products only as maker and SDS allow
Tool count, covers refitted, recorded before re-energising

essays.stem: Explain how you would handle the waste from an electrical installation job: copper and metal scrap, cable and PVC offcuts, packaging, fluorescent tubes and lamps, batteries and e-waste.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set up labelled containers before the job starts. Copper and other metal scrap goes in a secure container for recycling, because it has value and attracts theft. Useful lengths of cable and conduit are kept and labelled; small PVC offcuts and sheath go in general waste and are never burned, because burning PVC gives off toxic fumes. Cardboard and plastic packaging are flattened and bagged for recycling as the work goes. Fluorescent tubes and other lamps that contain mercury are kept whole in their boxes or a tube container and sent as hazardous waste. Lead-acid and other batteries are kept upright with terminals covered and returned to a licensed recycler or the supplier. E-waste such as old drivers and meters is kept for special collection. Waste is never left on the client's premises.
markingPoints: Labelled containers set up at the start
Copper and metal scrap secured for recycling
PVC offcuts and packaging handled correctly; no burning
Tubes kept whole as hazardous waste
Batteries and e-waste to licensed recyclers

essays.stem: Describe how cable, conduit, fittings, ladders and test instruments should be stored in an electrical store and workshop, and explain why.
essays.modelAnswer: Cable drums are stored on chocks or in a drum bay, with heavy drums at ground level, and part-used coils are tied, labelled with size and length and kept on racks, so the right cable is found and stock is known. Conduit and trunking lengths lie flat on racks, so they do not fall or bend and do not block walkways. Fittings and accessories go in labelled bins by size and type, with heavy boxes on lower shelves. Ladders are kept flat on wall brackets, out of the sun and rain, which can damage them. Test instruments are kept in their cases in a dry cupboard, with leads checked, because damp and knocks affect their accuracy and safety. Nothing is stored in front of switchboards, isolators, fire extinguishers or exits.
markingPoints: Drums chocked; coils tied and labelled on racks
Conduit and trunking flat on racks
Fittings in labelled bins, heavy items low
Ladders and instruments stored correctly, with reasons
Nothing in front of switchboards, isolators, extinguishers or exits

essays.stem: Explain how good housekeeping helps prevent electrical fires and electric shocks in a workshop or on site, and describe the checks you would make.
essays.modelAnswer: Electrical fires often start where heat meets something that burns. Keeping dust, paper, packaging and offcuts away from boards, light fittings and heaters removes the fuel. Fully unwinding cable reels and not overloading adaptors stops leads overheating. Filings and offcuts left inside boards can cause short circuits, so boards are cleaned before switch-on. Shocks are prevented by keeping leads off the floor where they get crushed, replacing damaged plugs and covers, fitting blanks in boards and keeping water away from electrical equipment. My checks would include: boards closed and blanked, clear space in front of them, leads in good condition and not trailing, no damaged outlets or covers, no combustible waste near heat, extinguishers in place, and isolators easy to reach. Faults are tagged and reported.
markingPoints: Removes fuel from near heat sources
Prevents overheated leads (reels unwound, no overloading)
Clean boards free of filings
Prevents shock: damaged leads, covers, blanks, water
Lists sensible checks and tags or reports faults

essays.stem: A fluorescent tube breaks in a classroom during a relamping job. Describe what you would do.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stop work and ask everyone to leave the area, keeping people from walking through the glass. I would open the windows and doors and switch off any fan or air conditioning that could spread the vapour, and let the room air for at least 10 to 15 minutes, or as the Centre's procedure says. Wearing gloves, I would scoop up the glass and powder with stiff card, pick up small pieces with sticky tape, and wipe the area with a damp paper towel. I would not use a vacuum or broom, as they spread the powder. Everything goes in a sealed bag or jar, labelled as broken lamp waste, and is stored with hazardous waste. I would then wash my hands, report the breakage and note how it happened so it can be avoided.
markingPoints: Clears the area of people
Ventilates; turns off fans or air conditioning
Gloves; card, tape and damp towel, no vacuum or broom
Seals and labels waste as hazardous
Washes hands, reports and reviews the cause

essays.stem: Write a housekeeping checklist of at least six items for the electrical training bays, and explain why each item is on it.
essays.modelAnswer: One: all board and box covers fitted and blanks in place, so no live parts can be touched. Two: training bay isolators clearly labelled and not blocked, so power can be cut quickly. Three: no cable offcuts, insulation or screws on the floor, which cause slips. Four: tools returned to the shadow board and counted, so none are lost or left inside equipment. Five: extension leads and test leads undamaged and coiled away, so they do not cause shocks or trips. Six: waste in the right bins, with copper scrap secured and tubes kept whole, so waste is recycled or disposed of safely. Seven: fire extinguisher in place and in date, for a quick response. Each item is ticked or marked with the action needed, a name and a date.
markingPoints: At least six sensible items
Electrical safety items (covers, blanks, isolators, leads)
Slip and trip items
Tool control and waste items
Reason for each item and a way of recording actions

essays.stem: Explain the safe use and storage of cleaning chemicals used in electrical work, such as contact cleaner, solvent wipes and battery acid neutraliser.
essays.modelAnswer: Before using any chemical I read its label and the safety data sheet, to know its hazards, the PPE needed and what to do in a spill or if it gets on skin or in the eyes. Contact cleaners and solvents are often flammable, so they are only used on isolated equipment, away from sparks and heat, with good ventilation. I wear gloves and safety glasses as the SDS says. I use only the amount needed and never mix products. Chemicals are kept in their original labelled containers, never in drink bottles, closed tightly and stored in a ventilated cabinet away from heat. Battery acid neutraliser is kept with the spill kit near the batteries. Empty cans and used wipes are disposed of as the label says, not burned. Any splash is washed off at once and reported.
markingPoints: Reads label and SDS first
Flammable: isolated equipment, no ignition, ventilation
PPE and no mixing
Stored closed and labelled in original containers in a ventilated cabinet
Correct disposal and first aid for splashes

essays.stem: As team leader, explain how you would get a team of trainees to keep up good housekeeping on a site job, and what you would do if one member does not.
essays.modelAnswer: I would explain at the start why housekeeping matters on an electrical job: it prevents trips, cuts, shocks and fires, and it is part of the quality the client sees. I would plan it into the job, with bins, bags and storage set up and time allowed at each break and at the end of the day, and give each person their own area to keep clear. I would lead by example and praise good work. I would check at set times using a short checklist. If one member keeps leaving a mess, I would speak to them privately, find out if there is a reason, explain the risk again and agree what I expect. I would then check their area more often. If it still did not improve, I would record it and report it to the supervisor.
markingPoints: Explains why housekeeping matters
Plans bins, storage, time and areas
Leads by example and checks with a checklist
Deals privately and fairly with a member who does not comply
Follows up, records and escalates if needed

essays.stem: Explain how temporary supplies and extension leads should be set up, used and cleared away on a job so they do not become hazards.
essays.modelAnswer: Temporary supplies are taken only from a point protected by a suitable breaker and earth leakage protection (a GFCI or RCD), as the Centre's rules say. Leads are checked before use for damaged sheaths, plugs and sockets, and any faulty lead is tagged out. Leads are routed along walls or overhead, not across walkways or through doorways where they can be crushed, and are protected with covers where they must cross a route. Cable reels are fully unwound for heavy loads so they do not overheat, and adaptors are not overloaded. Leads are kept out of water. At the end of the day, leads are unplugged, coiled loosely and stored dry, and the temporary supply is switched off and made safe. Damaged leads are reported and removed from use.
markingPoints: Supply from a protected point with earth leakage protection
Leads inspected; faulty ones tagged out
Routed away from walkways or protected; kept dry
Reels unwound; no overloading
Unplugged, coiled and stored; supply made safe at the end

practical1.title: Make safe and clean up an electrical training bay at the end of a job
practical1.brief: The assessor sets up a training bay as it might be left half-way through a job: loose cable ends, a missing breaker with no blank, filings inside the board, offcuts and packaging on the floor, tools left on a ladder, trailing leads and a broken (taped and bagged) tube to dispose of. As a group, plan the make-safe and clean-up, then carry it out. The bay is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked before and after. Each member takes charge of one part: making cable ends safe, fitting blanks and covers, cleaning the board with a non-metallic vacuum nozzle, sorting waste into the right containers, or storing tools, leads and materials. Finish by completing a make-safe and housekeeping checklist and reporting what is off and what is safe. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Training bay set up by the assessor with planted housekeeping faults
Lock-off kit, tags, voltage tester and proving unit
Insulated end caps or connectors and blanking plates
Vacuum cleaner with non-metallic nozzle and soft brush
Labelled waste containers: copper scrap, general, recycling, hazardous (tubes)
Gloves, safety glasses and dust masks
photos: The bay as found, before any work
The bay isolated, locked off and tagged, with the tester on the proving unit
Cable ends made safe and blanks fitted
Waste sorted into the labelled containers
Tools, leads and materials stored away
checklist: Followed safe isolation with a tester checked before and after
Made cable ends safe and fitted blanks and covers correctly
Cleaned the board with a non-metallic nozzle, not compressed air
Sorted waste correctly, keeping the tube waste whole and sealed
Stored tools, leads and materials in their proper places
Led their part clearly and helped others
Completed the checklist and reported the state of the bay
safety: Work only on the isolated, locked-off and tagged bay
Wear gloves and safety glasses when handling filings, glass and offcuts
Do not vacuum or sweep broken tube glass; it stays sealed in its bag
Keep walkways clear while the work goes on

practical2.title: Set up the electrical store and waste station, then run a housekeeping inspection
practical2.brief: Part A: as a group, organise the electrical store or a section of it. Rack conduit and trunking flat, tie and label part-used cable coils with size and length, put fittings into labelled bins with heavy items low, store ladders on brackets, and set up a waste station with labelled containers for copper scrap, recycling, general waste and hazardous waste (tubes, batteries, e-waste). Part B: write a housekeeping checklist for the electrical workshop and training bays, use it to inspect the area, and write an action list giving each fault an owner and a date. Each member organises one section and inspects one area. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Access to the electrical store and workshop
Labels, markers, cable ties and tags
Bins or containers for fittings and for each waste type
Blank checklist and action list forms
photos: The store before it is organised
Conduit racked and cable coils labelled
The finished waste station with labelled containers
A member inspecting an area with the checklist
The action list with owners and dates
checklist: Stored materials safely and in a sensible order
Labelled stock clearly with size and type
Set up the waste station correctly, with hazardous waste kept apart
Kept the space in front of boards, isolators, extinguishers and exits clear
Gave each action an owner and a date
safety: Lift safely; use a trolley for heavy boxes and drums
Chock cable drums when they are moved
Wear gloves when handling sheet metal, conduit and scrap
Do not open any board or remove any cover during the inspection
